keyFacts: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman is offering VIP packages ranging from $25,000 to $100,000 for donors at her upcoming inauguration.
The funds raised will support the official swearing-in ceremony, a private reception, and free public community celebrations.
Raman is scheduled to take office on December 14 while facing challenges including a budget crisis and homelessness.
body: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman is rolling out the red carpet for deep-pocketed donors willing to shell out as much as $100,000 for VIP perks at her inauguration.

An inaugural fundraising invitation obtained by the California Post reveals three “contribution” packages ranging from $25,000 to $100,000, offering reserved seating, access to a private reception and photo ops.
The top-tier $100,000 package offers donors 16 reserved seats at the Dec. 13 swearing-in ceremony and eight passes to an exclusive inaugural reception, complete with a photo op.
Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Thanks for signing up!
Advertisement
For $50,000, donors receive eight reserved seats and four reception passes. The lowest contribution tier, at $25,000, includes four reserved seats and two reception passes.
Advertisement
All three packages include dedicated check-in and recognition as inaugural committee members.
Contributions will support a fund dubbed “The People’s Mayor Inaugural Fund,” with the inauguration carrying the slogan “A City That Works, for Everyone.”
“We want her inauguration to look like the city that elected her: ambitious, joyful, and built by and for the people of Los Angeles,” the invitation reads.
Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters
Raman’s fundraising approach stands in contrast to that of her predecessor and a fellow democratic socialist.
Mayor Karen Bass’ team told the California Post that Bass did not offer similar donor packages for her 2022 inauguration.

Meanwhile, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani raised more than $3.8 million to fund his transition and inauguration, nearly $2 million more than either of his two predecessors collected during the first two months of their transitions, according to City & State New York.
Advertisement
Raman’s fundraising appeal seeks to bankroll the official swearing-in ceremony, a private reception and free community celebrations open to the public.
The invitation also opens the door to business contributions, noting that those donations will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.
Raman will take office Dec. 14, inheriting a city grappling with a budget crisis, mounting public safety costs and a worsening street homelessness crisis.
Advertisement
An estimated 45,194 people were experiencing homelessness in Los Angeles in 2026, including 29,115 living without shelter. Unsheltered homelessness jumped 7.9% from the previous year.

Raman has pledged to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least 50% before the 2028 Olympics, giving her roughly 19 months to deliver on one of her biggest campaign promises.

According to the invitation, inaugural contributions will be publicly disclosed as “behested payments,” a category of payments solicited by public officials for charitable, legislative or governmental purposes.
Advertisement

Unlike traditional campaign contributions, behested payments are not subject to contribution limits under state law. However, payments totaling $5,000 or more from a single source in a calendar year must be publicly disclosed, according to the California Fair Political Practices Commission.
Raman’s inauguration is scheduled for Sunday, Dec. 13, in downtown Los Angeles. The Post reached out to Raman for comment.

articles.headline: Marvel's Iron Man might be planning to rear its head at The Game Awards, if EA Motive's updated website is any indication
keyFacts: Redditors noticed that EA Motive updated its official website ahead of The Game Awards.
Disney announced that viewers can expect major gaming announcements during the ceremony airing on December 10.
An unfinished trailer for the Iron Man game leaked on the internet this summer.
body: EA Motive's Iron Man game has been quietly cooking away for a few years now, but don't worry. The wait to finally, officially see the superhero romp in action might be over soon, at least if the developer's updated website - two weeks before The Game Awards, no less - is any indication.

Redditors today noticed that EA Motive's official website got a little makeover recently. It's not clear when exactly the tweaks were pushed through, but the Wayback Machine makes clear that it's definitely been updated.
A new website look is by no means confirmation of an imminent announcement, of course, but there are a few other bits of evidence that certainly point in that direction.

For one, The Game Awards 2026 will air on Disney Plus for the very first time, alongside all the other platforms you're used to. "As the evening unfolds, viewers can expect major announcements and surprises from some of Disney's most anticipated titles in gaming," the film studio said earlier this month.
Kingdom Hearts 4, Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra and more are definitely possible, too. Turmoil at Marvel's Blade developer Arkane Lyon makes that one a tricker guess, however.

Second is the fact that The Game Awards air on 10th December - eight days before the global opening of Avengers: Doomsday, a film that's shaping up to become the biggest cinematic event since the last time Marvel chucked all of its toys into the same sandbox and bashed them together. Giving one of the company's most popular superheroes the spotlight around the same time seems like a good idea.

This isn't the first time EA's Iron Man has popped up in recent times, either. What appeared to be an unfinished trailer for Motive's Iron Man leaked onto the internet this summer, and showed off blisteringly fast flying and lots of destructive gadgets. It looked further along than I expected, at least, so I wouldn't be surprised to see the billionaire playboy philanthropist rear his head again in two weeks time.

articles.headline: The PC specs for Mass Effect-like RPG Exodus are basically bearable for a blockbuster space opera in 2026
keyFacts: The publisher revealed the PC system specifications for the upcoming space role-playing game Exodus.
Playing the game at 1080p and 30 frames per second requires a minimum of an Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 and an Nvidia RTX 2060 or AMD RX 6600.
The game is scheduled for release on April 7, 2027, though the publisher noted that hardware specifications may change prior to launch.
body: Between Matthew McConaughey, the flesh cathedrals, the space bears, FemJun and the tragedy of Biggs "The Bolt" Keil, the pre-release reveals for Mass Effect-like space RPG Exodus have been a real emotional rollercoaster. It's almost disappointing to learn that the recommended PC system specs are just sort of… fine. Broadly within expectations, by 2026 standards, anyway.

True, you'll need one of those Nvidia RTX 5080 things if you want to play it in 4K at 60fps, but the True Gamer understands that 4K/60FPS is a dangerous and blasphemical overreach, akin to building the Tower of Babel out of cats. 1080p/30FPS was perfectly good enough for Virtua Tennis 3 on Xbox 360, and it'll be perfectly good enough for this game about *squints*… octopus mercenaries. For that, you'll only need an i5-10400, an Nvidia 2060 and a mere 16GB of RAM. Granted, I think new PCs with those components currently cost $200,000, but that isn't Exodus's fault. It's that Jensen Huang who's to blame. Here's the complete spec rundown, anyway.
Minimum (1080p at 30 FPS)
- CPU: Intel Core i5-10400 or AMD Ryzen 5 3600
- GPU: Nvidia RTX 2060 6GB or AMD RX 6600 8GB
- RAM: 16GB dual-channel
- Storage: 110GB SATA SSD
Recommended (1440p at 60 FPS)
- CPU: Intel Core i7-11700 or AMD Ryzen 5 7600
- GPU: Nvidia RTX 3080 10 GB or AMD RX 7700 XT 12GB
- RAM: 16GB dual-channel
- Storage: 110GB (NVMe SSD preferred)
4K (2160p at 60 FPS)
- CPU: Intel Core Ultra 7 265K or AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D
- GPU: Nvidia RTX 5080 16GB or AMD RX 9070 XT 16GB
- RAM: 32GB dual-channel
- Storage: 110GB (NVMe SSD preferred)

Will you be playing Exodus? I think it looks swankier so far than Owlcat's surprisingly unconvincing The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, that other great hope of people who mourn Mass Effect 5, but I haven't spent any time with a build. It's out 7th April 2027 - I imagine these recommended specs might alter as they stuff in more McConaughey and layer up the space bears.

- Archetype go all in on the Mass Effect vibes with a FemJun reveal, but I'm just left hoping they'll call the alternative option MascJun to balance it out
- Exodus will likely win the Mass Effect spiritual successor war, thanks partly to its Cool Octopus, but I think it has a boring hero problem

articles.headline: Smartphone shipments face another bleak year before modest 2028 comeback
keyFacts: Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, according to Counterpoint Research.
Counterpoint Research stated that rising memory costs and constrained supplies driven by AI server demands are putting pressure on handset makers.
Counterpoint forecasts a 6 percent market rebound in 2028 as memory supplies improve and pricing begins to stabilize.
body: Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028.

That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker , which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers.

The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market.

Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns.

The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC , memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing.

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones.

Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported , memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026.

For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases.
"The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang.

"Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets."
Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years.
Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing.

A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery.

"The unusually low 2027 base creates the potential for a robust rebound in 2028 once the memory bottleneck begins to ease. But this should not be interpreted as a return to the old market trajectory," Wang said.
"Some low-end demand has been permanently lost, and the 2028 market will still be about 14 percent below 2025 shipments."
Potential availability of 6G-capable smartphones toward the end of the decade could give the market a boost, but Counterpoint does not expect it to regain its 2025 shipment levels by 2030. ®

articles.headline: Will we ever see another game like GTA VI?
keyFacts: Rockstar Games reported that Grand Theft Auto VI earned nearly $3.8 billion on its first day of release.
Video game journalist Chris Plante said the title arrives during industry-wide layoffs, rising development budgets, and growing debates over artificial intelligence.
Rockstar will prioritize launching Grand Theft Auto Online and potentially expanding the game before developing a future sequel, Plante stated.
body: Grand Theft Auto VI arrived last week, 13 years after the last installment in the series, to an enormous debut — nearly $3.8 billion in its first day, according to developer Rockstar Games. That’s more than Avengers: Endgame has earned at the global box office across its entire theatrical run, including rereleases.

The game took more than eight years to develop, and Rockstar grew to more than 4,700 employees worldwide during production. In the game, players are catapulted into Leonida, a fictional version of Florida that includes Vice City, the series’ take on Miami.

Unlike past games in the series, you play as a couple, Jason and Lucia, who are trying to make enough money to support their young family and make it out. Maintaining their relationship is just as important as robbing stores or completing missions.

For all that GTA VI is shaping up to be a critically acclaimed triumph, however, it arrives at a difficult moment for the video game industry. Studios have endured years of layoffs and rising development costs, while workers worry about how generative AI could affect their jobs and creative work. Can an industry under this much pressure afford to keep making games this big, or is GTA VI doomed to be the last of its kind?

To find out, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Chris Plante, a video game journalist with about two decades of experience and host of the podcast Post Games . They discussed GTA VI’s long road to release, what could be next for the franchise and whether DLC is on the horizon, and the future of blockbuster gaming more broadly.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .
Chris, people are saying that this game is the last of its kind. Why are they saying that?

It kind of is, but I think we should be really specific when we say that. The last of its kind means the last of this: thousands and thousands of people trying to make one game without artificial intelligence, and it being a historic, all-consuming moment.

The best shot that we have of another game like this happening is GTA VII. But what I would be wary of is saying there aren’t going to be big-budget video games anymore. If you look at another game that came out just this month, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a remake of one of the most famous games ever, one of the most beloved games ever, and it looks stunning. It’s on the Nintendo Switch 2. It is great. And it cost a fraction of what Grand Theft Auto cost [to make]. It took a fraction of the time to create. And yet it still feels absolutely decadent.

You know what a fair comparison would be? We get those Avatar movies — they take forever because they cost a fortune to make, they require all this new technology. That’s your Grand Theft Auto. But you wouldn’t look at an Avatar and say, ‘Well, they’re never going to make expensive movies anymore.’ We still get Dune . We still get Marvel movies. Those things are still happening.

There is a whole separate question about the stability of the highest ends of the industry, the companies that tried to be the Grand Theft Autos: Electronic Arts, the company that makes Madden; companies like Xbox, which owns Activision, which makes Call of Duty.

You might notice I’m saying a lot of which does this but owns that. The consolidation in the industry is real, and it’s a real problem. So there’s going to be turmoil, but it is not the end of video games, and it’s not even the end of big video games.
It sounds like this is a great time for the industry, but it’s actually the opposite.

It’s a great time for people who play video games and a nightmare time for people who make video games. If you play video games right now, you can turn on Steam, which is a storefront on PC, and you can find literally hundreds of games that were released just this week. Over a thousand new games are released every month on Steam. And because of that, it targets not every niche, but close. There is probably something out there for you.

This is a nightmare for people who make games because even Grand Theft Auto, when it comes to PC, is going to live right alongside all those other games. So for the people who do not have the name recognition, who do not have the marketing, you can launch a game that you spent tens, maybe hundreds of millions of dollars on, and it is going to, the same day that it comes out, compete against a brand-new $5 game that was made by three or four people with a whole bunch of contractor support for a very low cost and has just as good of odds, minus the marketing, of being a hit.

Is AI going to make it less risky for big gaming companies to invest in developing something ambitious because maybe they can make it dramatically cheaper and compete with the games that only cost $10 to develop?
AI, as the investment class has it in their head: The answer is no, not whatsoever.
“Looking even beyond games, there’s a lot of reason to be cautious about things that seem like they’re going to make things faster actually, in the long term, making them much slower.”

AI as a tool, it gets more complicated. I think when a lot of people hear AI, they think, I’ve seen a video where I can go on Google and type a prompt, and I say, give me Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but make it like a Black Eyed Peas concert. And people are like, wow, you seem really out of touch, but I’ll make it for you anyway . And then you have this great game, and you are getting the party started in here. And that is not how any of this works at all.

Games are literally a miracle. My former colleague, Frank Lantz, who’s an educator and game designer, would compare it to art, if you also had to build a skyscraper or a highway. You have to both make the architecture and make the art. It’s unhinged. We do not have this world where games just are going to materialize.

Now where it gets really complicated and it gets really messy inside the industry is using AI tools for things like coding. And this is very controversial amongst a certain corner of video games culture and video game developers. There are people who want a full ban, that we are not using AI on anything, that we need to protect jobs, and that it shouldn’t be used for generating images or art or music or code.

And then there are people who say, but I use AI for code. I think it is relatively common, and that is somewhat of a controversial take, but it is what I hear from so many people I talk to who are on that side of game development, to be using it when you are programming as a tool.

I think there’s a lot of promises, but I think that, again, looking even beyond games, there’s a lot of reason to be cautious about things that seem like they’re going to make things faster actually, in the long term, making them much slower.
And we still live in a world where it makes sense to start developing a GTA VII?
It does for Rockstar for sure, though I don’t think that they will be in a rush to do it anytime soon, for a few reasons.

One, they still need to get Grand Theft Auto Online out. That’s where the real money is. Grand Theft Auto Online drops people into the city of each new game. Grand Theft Auto V did it with LA. Now you’re going to have it in Miami. And that is where people can get lost for years and years and years, and they can start charging you for little incremental things like cool new outfits or fancy cars or spots to live. So that’s going to be their priority.

There has been word or rumor that they might just expand Grand Theft Auto VI, that we would see more cities. Who knows if that’s true? It would be a different approach, but the game began as a thing called Project Americas and was supposed to be a much larger game. So that could be one way that it grows rather than a GTA VII: We just see a GTA VI that gets bigger and bigger, not unlike Fortnite, but we’re going to get more of it.
Do you want to put in an early guess as to what year GTA VII comes out so that someone listening to this in, I don’t know, 10, 15, 20 years can be like, wow, that guy nailed it ?

Damn. Actually, I was going to say that I think it would be sooner than 13 years, and I’m not sure I actually believe that. I’m going to put it at, let’s say, 2037. I’ll see you in 11 years. Does that sound good?
If all goes well for our industries, yes.
Yeah. Better odds in the Grand Theft Auto business. I mean, hey, we can always turn into a romantic duo performing a life of crime.

articles.headline: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
keyFacts: French authorities ordered actor Gérard Depardieu to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting actress Charlotte Arnould.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, particularly in the arts.
Depardieu denies the rape allegations, and his lawyer said he disputes the ruling without specifying if he will appeal.
body: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.
Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

articles.headline: The last refuges for endangered animals are becoming disaster zones
keyFacts: Roughly 300 Mariana crows survive today on the island of Rota, down from thousands due to habitat loss and invasive species.
Conservationists saved 13 captive Mariana crows by moving them indoors before Category 5 Super Typhoon Bavi destroyed the outdoor aviaries.
Researchers said intensifying extreme weather and funding threats put delicate conservation efforts and endangered species at ongoing risk.
body: When the Mariana crow calls, it’s taken as a warning.

To the Indigenous CHamoru people of the Mariana Islands, the bird is known as the Åga, an ancestral messenger who alerts the community of impending illness or weather disaster. In the dense canopy of Rota’s limestone forest, where the Mariana crow lives, it is a gardener — a key seed disperser from which the lush canopy grows.

According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service , the species is endemic to Guam and the nearby island of Rota, a US territory, which means they live nowhere else on Earth. They once numbered in the thousands. But over the past 60 years, they have vanished from Guam and dwindled on Rota. Roughly 300 survive today.

Now teetering on the brink of extinction, every remaining Mariana crow represents a fragile ecosystem and a deep cultural lineage the islands cannot afford to lose. Researchers from the University of Washington and ecologists from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance are working tirelessly to make sure that doesn’t happen.

The effort to prevent the bird’s precipitous decline in the wild has been underway for more than two decades. Beginning in 2005 with field monitoring and observation, researchers realized they would have to step in and raise the birds in human-assisted aviaries to save the species. By 2016, teams collected their first clutch of wild eggs and successfully released the first cohort back into the forest the following year. In the years since, the active recovery program has bred dozens of birds in captivity and has given the wild population a boost that researchers hope the birds can eventually sustain on their own — all made possible through millions of dollars in federal grants and academic funding, decades of field research, and tight coordination among local and federal partners.

But in July, the entire effort was endangered by one of the most drastic events to hit the region in years. For days, Category 5 Super Typhoon Bavi pummeled the island. As it barreled down, conservationists realized they needed to act fast and save the species, so they assembled makeshift indoor aviaries inside the scientists’ quarters on the research base. The small crew boarded up windows and stocked up on food. Only weeks into their new lives in the forest, the crows were back inside. Their caretakers would ride out the storm beside them.
The decision saved the flock.

The team successfully brought 13 birds to safety before the storm hit. Of the nine that weren’t captured, two died, and one was emaciated and had a minor wing injury from the storm. The rest of the wild population took a hit, too, though researchers are still accounting for the total loss. The toll on the ongoing conservation work was profound. Bavi obliterated the facility’s outdoor aviaries, leaving an exhausted crew to care for the agitated Mariana crow in a compound that still remains without power just as another storm, Category 4 Typhoon Champi, passed through the islands in mid-October.

Ecologist Sarah Faegre, the primary investigator for the University of Washington’s Rota Avian Behavioral Ecology Program, was there to assess the damage. The enormous aviary, which her own father, an architect, built more than a decade ago, had survived its fair share of typhoons. But last month, it lay collapsed. “It was heartbreaking,” she told me. “It nearly made me cry.” The massive, industrial-grade plastic pipe frame that held the aviary together, Faegre said, “looked like a pile of broken bones.”
Around the world, countless endangered animals are a single disaster from absolute collapse.

Decades of habitat loss, shifting climate and degrading ecosystems have pushed much of the planet’s biodiversity to precariously low populations. But advances in science and conservation have yielded remarkable recoveries: The Endangered Species Act alone has clawed back nearly 300 species — the bald eagle, humpback whale, and grizzly bear among them — from the precipice.

Still, the survival of many more animals today faces a dangerous bottleneck — sometimes it’s just a single aviary, a small team of researchers, and a modest pot of funding that stands in the way of extinction.

At the same time, shifting political tides threaten to undermine those efforts even further. In the US, the Trump administration has slashed the very funding that could help an effort like breeding the Mariana crows recover from a major storm.

“If we’re no longer able to access funding and take action to do restoration work, it’s less likely that the species will ever recover and be able to be removed from the [endangered species] list,” said Sara Gottlieb, with the Nature Conservancy.

With such existential challenges, it’s worth questioning why Faegre and others are so dedicated to saving the Mariana crow population. But in late October, even in the midst of Bavi’s aftermath, the research team discovered something hopeful.
A precarious moment

The Mariana Islands, a 15-island archipelago that includes the US territories of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, are regularly hit with tropical storms. But for generations, the Mariana crow was able to persist in the remote, northern island of Rota — a model of a small, resilient ecosystem in part because its geography has protected it from the most severe disasters.

“Rota and the Mariana crow have seen many typhoons throughout history and have proven resilience,” said Phillip Hannon, research coordinator for the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance’s Mariana crow rear-and-release program. “The jungle, too, regenerates very quickly in the heat and humidity of a tropical island.”

But as climate change has fueled more frequent and severe storms, even the historically buffered areas are more exposed than ever. And this year, abnormally warm ocean temperatures in the Pacific have caused an unusual clustering of typhoon activity this year .
Why I reported this story
I was born and raised on Saipan in the Northern Mariana Islands, a US territory just north of Guam, where military presence was simply a backdrop of growing up.
But long before concrete runways carved up our native coral limestone, these islands thrived with unique flora and fauna that filled the forest canopy with song.

Today, many of the species our ancestors knew survive mostly in oral histories and local legends — the kinds of stories I grew up hearing. Centuries of colonial expansion, military construction, and the escalating climate crisis have fractured these isolated ecosystems, quieting once-bustling forests into fragments of their natural heritage.
I wanted to tell this story because it is a rare hopeful one — even despite the ongoing threats to the restoration of the Åga.

For the Mariana crow, the situation was already grave. The population was completely wiped out from Guam by the late 1990s and early 2000s after a new predator, the brown tree snake — introduced into Guam via World War II military cargo ships — devastated native nests. With Guam’s population gone, the species’ survival now hinges entirely on Rota, a 33-square-mile island north of Guam where severe typhoons repeatedly thrash the native forest canopy the species uses for nesting.

But intensifying super typhoons are striking an ecosystem already fractured by habitat loss and invasive species from rampant militarization. With every storm hitting an already diminished population, the work of conservationists is a crucial step to buy more time so that wildlife can eventually rebound on its own.

The joint Mariana crow recovery project by the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance (SDZWA), the University of Washington, and local partners across Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands has boosted the population from its lowest — just roughly 130 individuals — to 300 birds, 79 of which were reared and reintroduced by SDZWA.

But this conservation breeding approach is “a method of last resort” only used when a species is on the absolute brink of extinction, like the California condor or the Hawaiian crow known as ‘Alalā, said Ronald Swaisgood, director of recovery ecology at the San Diego Zoo.

“All of these species absolutely depend on the critical habitat; otherwise, they’ll all be in breeding centers, and none will be in the wild,” Swaisgood said. “But sometimes that’s where we unfortunately finish because increasingly more species require this kind of infrastructure, which is very costly, but it’s our only remaining tool to prevent extinction of some of these species.”

Although it might sound like a long shot, many of these last-resort strategies have had real success. In East Tennessee, ecologists successfully recovered the Smoky Madtom . In the 1980s, decades after the tiny, nocturnal Smoky Madtom catfish was accidentally wiped out of its native creek, a researcher named Gerry Dinkins rediscovered a fragile surviving population. With the help of federal funding, scientists gathered a handful of wild eggs during the summer spawning season, brought them back to the lab to incubate, then nurtured the fragile fry in specialized aquariums, away from predators and other threats. Once the young madtoms were strong enough to fend for themselves, they carried them back to their native home in Abrams Creek, slipping them into the water at night to match their nocturnal habits and keep hungry birds and larger fish at bay.
Decades of work to save a species can unravel in a single disaster
Saving a species from extinction can take decades. A single storm or wildfire can put that work in jeopardy.

Consider the eastern hellbender, North America’s largest amphibian. Its population has declined by nearly 80 percent , even as conservationists have spent years raising young hellbenders for release, monitoring populations, and pushing for federal protection. Then, in 2024, Hurricane Helene tore through critical river habitat in the Appalachians, washing some of the aquatic salamanders onto land, where they cannot survive. The destruction coincided with their fall breeding season, threatening the next generation, too.

The storm underscored the urgency of protecting the hellbender. But a proposed Endangered Species Act listing remained stalled, leaving recovery efforts without the full support of federal safeguards.

And then in Hawaii, another disaster nearly severed a species’ lifeline. The ʻAlalā, or Hawaiian crow, was already extinct in the wild when the 2023 Maui wildfires approached a facility housing birds essential to its recovery. Staff fought back the flames with hoses until emergency crews arrived. No birds were harmed, but their survival depended on people holding the fire at bay.
Protecting the birds in captivity is only part of the challenge. Returning them to the wild requires healthy, protected forests — and sustained funding to manage those lands.

These narrow escapes reveal a growing vulnerability in conservation: As climate change intensifies extreme weather, the places keeping imperiled species alive can themselves become disaster zones. Years of painstaking recovery work increasingly depend on whether those fragile refuges can withstand the next catastrophe.

These surviving populations provide more time to address the core causes of long-term decline. A 2020 US Fish and Wildlife Service review warned that climate change poses a growing long-term threat to the Smoky Madtom, as rising temperatures and extreme droughts dry up critical stream habitats. Severe low-water events, like the 2016 drought that left up to half of Citico Creek bone-dry, could endanger the catfish by disrupting nesting, reducing reproduction, and increasing mortality.

“Anything that significantly changes the habitat condition in the area, including catastrophic storms causing large areas of tree blow-downs and landslides or wildfire leading to sudden inputs of sediments or toxins into the streams where these fish live could result in major impacts to the species,” Gottlieb said.
All it takes is one wild nest

After Champi passed in mid-October, Faegre was walking through Rota’s forests when she spotted an encouraging sign that a Mariana crow — that had been reintroduced into the forest years ago — had left behind: a single, modest nest.

It was one of the first that researchers found in October since Bavi made landfall. The island’s canopy remains noticeably more patchy and open than the Mariana crow’s preferred dense nesting habitat, but Faegre watched a released trio — made up of two males and an unrelated female — actively collecting roots and plant fibers, putting the finishing touches on a nest that’s now nearly complete.

Because the crows typically begin nesting in August, researchers were unsure if they would attempt to breed at all this season. Yet despite the compromised environment and a delayed start, Faegre said if all goes well, the throuple — as the team has taken to calling them — could lay eggs in a week or two.

Nearly two weeks after Bavi battered the island, the Mariana crows that researchers scrambled to save during the worst days of the storm were rereleased into the wild. Fallen trees and downed power poles blocked the roads, delaying the birds’ return. In the meantime, the team built emergency outdoor aviaries to get the birds back outside. But with island power knocked out for months, survival became a logistical battle, Faegre said. The facility relied on a generator to preserve the crows’ food, running it just a few hours a day to stretch scarce fuel. When the freezer food eventually spoiled, the team turned to shelf-stable rations and later called on partners in Guam to ship in the fresh food the crows desperately needed.

“Bavi was an incredibly powerful storm, much worse than any in the living memory of the people of Rota,” Faegre said. “To this day, more than three months later, the Mariana crow facility and many homes on Rota remain without power,” adding that some of the crew members with power are storing the Mariana crow’s food at their homes.

Just before Bavi struck, the team was already caring for eight injured Mariana crow. Two were previously released birds recovering from injuries sustained during Super Typhoon Sinlaku, a Category 5 storm that hit just months earlier. According to Faegre, injured crows are typically transferred for rehabilitation and eventual rerelease. But due to the severity of the injuries, six of the birds could not return to their native habitat and were relocated to the St. Louis Zoo early this month.

Schoolchildren who took frequent field trips to the Rota facility named two of the relocated birds, according to Faegre. One named Suette means “lucky” in CHamoru, while another named Lina’la means “life.”

“The sentiment is that these birds were lucky and got a second chance at life,” Faegre said. “Suette, for example, tackled a crab that was a bit too big for him when he was a young bird in the wild. He lost a wing to the crab but has done very well in human care since then.”

As climate change accelerates, Swaisgood said relying on second chances won’t be enough. To ensure the Mariana crow survives the next storm and thrives beyond it, the team has been exploring new ways to diversify and expand the Mariana crow’s habitats across safer, more varied ecosystems like the neighboring Northern islands.

But to do so, they need funding. The program has already proven successful, with recent analyses indicating a modest recovery in the Mariana crow population and that the decline has stopped. Yet Swaisgood said appropriated federal funds are failing to reach them. “Several of our projects, the ones that depend on federal funding, are running out,” he said.

The question is whether nature can do so fast enough to survive more upheaval. While forests and habitats may eventually rebound, time is running out faster than evolution or natural recovery can match. Still, targeted conservation acts as an indispensable bridge to keep species hanging on while working towards larger systemic solutions.
“Everywhere in the world, including the environment, is always going to be impacted,” Gottlieb said. “But what we do see over and over is that these areas can recover. Sometimes even on their own.”
